items.text: In  the  digital  age,  personal  data  has  become  one  of  the  most valuable  commodities,  shaping  how  businesses,  governments, and  individuals interact. Every online search, social media post, and mobile transaction contributes to a vast ecosystem of data collection and analysis. Tech giants employ sophisticated algorithms  to  track  user  preferences,  predict  behavior,  and deliver  personalized advertisements that seem almost intuitive. While this data-driven world enhances convenience and efficiency, it simultaneously exposes individuals to unprecedented  privacy  risks.  The  boundaries  between  public and  private life are blurring as personal information becomes a tradable  asset,  often  exchanged  without  informed  consent. Governments argue that surveillance technologies are essential for national security and public safety, yet the same tools can be misused  to  monitor  citizens,  suppress  dissent,  or  manipulate elections. Data breaches and unauthorized access to confidential information have become  alarmingly frequent, eroding  public  trust  in digital institutions. In many cases, users agree  to  complex  privacy  policies  they  barely  read,  granting corporations  sweeping  rights  over  their  data  in  exchange  for 'free'  services.  This  imbalance  of  power  raises  critical  ethical questions:  Who  truly  owns  personal  data?  How  much

control should individuals retain over their digital footprints? Addressing these concerns requires a multi-dimensional approach. Stronger data protection laws, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), aim to empower  users  by ensuring transparency and consent. Similarly, initiatives in India like  the  Digital  Personal  Data Protection Act seek to safeguard citizens' privacy while enabling responsible innovation. However, legislation  alone  cannot  solve  the  problem.  Public  awareness, ethical  corporate  behavior,  and the promotion of digital literacy are equally vital. As technology continues to evolve-from facial recognition  to  artificial  intelligence-the ethical use of data will determine  the future of digital democracy. Ultimately, privacy in the  21st  century  is  not  just  a  legal  right  but  a  fundamental expression  of  personal  autonomy,  dignity,  and  freedom  in  an interconnected world

items.text: Deep beneath the ocean's surface lies one of the least explored frontiers  on  Earth  -  the  abyssal  plain.  Stretching  across  vast regions of the seabed, these flat, dark expanses are home to an array  of  organisms  uniquely  adapted  to  conditions of crushing pressure,  perpetual darkness, and scarce food supply. Life here thrives  not  on  sunlight  but  on  chemical  energy  derived  from hydrothermal  vents,  where  mineral-rich  fluids  gush  from  the Earth's crust. Around these vents, chemosynthetic bacteria form the  foundation  of  an  entire  ecosystem,  sustaining  giant  tube worms, blind shrimp, and specialised crabs.

items.text:
The  discovery  of  these vent-based ecosystems in the late 20th century revolutionised our understanding of life itself, challenging  the  long-held notion that sunlight was essential for biological  productivity.  The  study  of  such  organisms  has  also deepened  scientific  insight  into  possible  extraterrestrial  life, particularly  on  icy  moons  like  Europa  and  Enceladus,  where similar energy sources may exist beneath frozen crusts. Yet, the growing  interest  in  deep-sea  mining  threatens  to disturb these fragile  habitats.  Extraction  of  minerals  such  as  cobalt,  nickel, and  rare  earth  elements could irreversibly damage ecosystems that have taken millennia to evolve. Scientists urge that conservation  and  research  must precede exploitation, ensuring that curiosity does not turn into destruction.
SSC CGL 21/09/2025 (Shift 1)

texts.orig: In  the  digital  age,  personal  data  has  become  one  of  the  most valuable  commodities,  shaping  how  businesses,  governments, and  individuals interact. Every online search, social media post, and mobile transaction contributes to a vast ecosystem of data collection and analysis. Tech giants employ sophisticated algorithms  to  track  user  preferences,  predict  behavior,  and deliver  personalized advertisements that seem almost intuitive. While this data-driven world enhances convenience and efficiency, it simultaneously exposes individuals to unprecedented  privacy  risks.  The  boundaries  between  public and  private life are blurring as personal information becomes a tradable  asset,  often  exchanged  without  informed  consent. Governments argue that surveillance technologies are essential for national security and public safety, yet the same tools can be misused  to  monitor  citizens,  suppress  dissent,  or  manipulate elections. Data breaches and unauthorized access to confidential information have become  alarmingly frequent, eroding  public  trust  in digital institutions. In many cases, users agree  to  complex  privacy  policies  they  barely  read,  granting corporations  sweeping  rights  over  their  data  in  exchange  for 'free'  services.  This  imbalance  of  power  raises  critical  ethical questions:  Who  truly  owns  personal  data?  How  much  control should individuals retain over their digital footprints? Addressing these concerns requires a multi-dimensional approach. Stronger data protection laws, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), aim to empower  users  by ensuring transparency and consent. Similarly, initiatives in India like  the  Digital  Personal  Data Protection Act seek to safeguard citizens' privacy while enabling responsible innovation. However, legislation  alone  cannot  solve  the  problem.  Public  awareness, ethical  corporate  behavior,  and the promotion of digital literacy are equally vital. As technology continues to evolve-from facial recognition  to  artificial  intelligence-the ethical use of data will determine  the future of digital democracy. Ultimately, privacy in the  21st  century  is  not  just  a  legal  right  but  a  fundamental expression  of  personal  autonomy,  dignity,  and  freedom  in  an interconnected world

texts.orig: The  discovery  of  these vent-based ecosystems in the late 20th century revolutionised our understanding of life itself, challenging  the  long-held notion that sunlight was essential for biological  productivity.  The  study  of  such  organisms  has  also deepened  scientific  insight  into  possible  extraterrestrial  life, particularly  on  icy  moons  like  Europa  and  Enceladus,  where similar energy sources may exist beneath frozen crusts. Yet, the growing  interest  in  deep-sea  mining  threatens  to disturb these fragile  habitats.  Extraction  of  minerals  such  as  cobalt,  nickel, and  rare  earth  elements could irreversibly damage ecosystems that have taken millennia to evolve. Scientists urge that conservation  and  research  must precede exploitation, ensuring that curiosity does not turn into destruction.
